 Korea Open: Wang to Remember
 Wednesday, November 4, 2026
 TEXT BY DIANNE PIERRE | JNANESH SALIAN/BADMINTONPHOTO 
 SHARE 
 Wang Yu-Kai had studied his senior Chou Tien Chen for years. At YEOSU VICTOR Korea Open 2026 on Wednesday, he found a way past the world No.4 on his third attempt. 
 It was a match to remember too, as Wang produced the biggest upset of the opening round in toppling the top seed 21-18 16-21 21-12. The win marked a milestone for the youngster, who lost both their previous meetings in straight games.
 “You could consider it an achievement. My goal was to push my senior to three games,” the 22-year-old shared. “Having lost both the previous matches 2-0, I wanted to take this one to a deciding game and really give him a fight.”
 The victory was made all the more significant by Wang’s longstanding admiration for Chou, whose matches he watched while coming through the ranks.
 “I used to learn a lot watching his videos and I’ve also had the opportunity to train with him. He’s a very determined and dedicated player, so there are many aspects of his game and attitude I look up to and try to learn from.
 “This match has given me a lot more confidence for future competitions. I’ve gained a better understanding of how to approach similar situations in the future, how to respond to each rally and handle different shots.
 “During the match, I still found myself rushing things a little, especially when he started catching up. I became quite nervous at those moments. But after playing this match, I have a better idea of how to adjust and deal with these situations next time.”
 The win comfortably surpassed the target Wang had set for himself at the start of the week.
 “My original goal was simply to win at least one match in the main draw. Previously, when I made it through the qualifying rounds of a Super 500, I was eliminated in the Round of 32. So this result means a lot.”
 Next up is another fellow Chinese Taipei shuttler, Wang Tzu Wei, in the second round.
 “I might watch some of his matches again. I hope I can perform at my best, stay relaxed and avoid getting too nervous when facing my senior.”
 Yoo Delights Home Crowd 
 Yoo Tae Bin gave the home fans plenty to cheer about after defeating Indian veteran Prannoy H.S. 23-21 21-15.
 Playing in front of a partisan crowd, Yoo showed maturity beyond his years to edge a tense opening game before pulling away in the second. The Korean remained patient throughout, refusing to be drawn into forcing the issue against one of the tour’s giant hitters.
 “It was important to engage in longer rallies and be patient in my approach. He has a great deal of experience, so I tried not to rush things at any point.”
 Yoo entertained the home crowd in Yeosu. 
 The result was another encouraging step in what has already been a breakthrough season for Yoo, highlighted by his Asian Games bronze medal. He admitted there was extra motivation whenever he competed on home soil.
 “Tournaments in Korea have always meant a lot to me and they naturally make me want to be even more focused and give my best. I really want to achieve a good result here, so I put extra effort into preparing thoroughly beforehand.”
 Yoo’s measured style and movement have drawn comparisons with some leading names but the 22-year-old revealed the player he has learned the most from is Olympic champion Chen Long.
 “I’ve picked up many things from watching him. In that sense, Chen Long is a role model for me.”
 He will take on Yudai Okimoto on Thursday with a quarterfinal spot at stake.
